requiredDisclosures: Written notice must be given before filing eviction in Justice Court
Notice must state the specific grounds for eviction
Notice must be delivered: in person to tenant, to anyone 16+ at the property, by mail, or by affixing to inside of main entry door
Notice left on door must also be mailed on the same day
Landlord must provide written inventory of security deposit deductions within 30 days of move-out
illegalReasons: Tenant filed a complaint with a governmental entity about a building or housing code violation
Tenant established, attempted to establish, or participated in a tenant organization
Tenant exercised a right or remedy under Texas law
Tenant requested a repair in writing
Discrimination based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, or disability (Fair Housing Act)
Texas law: evicting to retaliate is illegal under Texas Property Code Section 92.331
retaliationProtections: Texas Property Code Section 92.331: landlord may not retaliate against tenant for good-faith exercise of rights
Retaliation presumed if landlord acts within 6 months after tenant exercised rights
Tenant may terminate lease, withhold rent, or sue for a civil penalty of 1 month's rent + $500 + attorney fees if retaliation proven
notes: Texas has no statewide rent control — preempted by state law
Landlord must make repairs that materially affect health or safety if tenant gives written notice
Tenant may repair-and-deduct up to 1 month's rent if landlord fails to make required repairs
Writ of possession (lockout) can be executed 24 hours after judgment — very fast process in Texas
Security deposit must be returned within 30 days of move-out with written itemization of deductions
Landlord must provide working smoke detectors — failure may be a defense
Texas Justice Court eviction process (forcible entry and detainer) is county-level
